items.title: AI Is Getting Good at Math. Here’s Why.
items.author: Ankit Maloo
items.excerpt: In May, an internal model at OpenAI found a counterexample to Erdős's unit distance conjecture. Open since 1946. Many experts had tried to prove it. OpenAI found a counterexample instead. A month later, OpenAI published a proof of the Cycle Double Cover (CDC) problem, then solutions to ten more open problems by July. And a proof of Navier Stokes in September. Anthropic published a formalization of the fermat's last theorem, and advanced bounds on Reimann's hypothesis. The models are suddenly good at math. The question that interests me is whether we can predict what kinds of problems these models will solve. What makes a problem tractable for an LLM, and what do these solutions have in common? If AI solves problems differently from humans, identifying the difference should help us decide where to point it. The unit-distance disproof has the richest commentary, so let’s start there. Problem complexity Here is a simple mental model. To solve any given problem, you need a sequence of hints or insights with work between them. This maps surprisingly well to simple everyday problems and to complex ideas like General Relativity1 (see Bonus). The sequence looks something like this: Insight -> time / effort -> insight -> time/effort -> solution. An expert would need fewer hints than a beginner would, as they would have more background. In his commentary on unit-distance proof, WT Gowers uses a similar idea: the difficulty of the proof is the shortest sequence of hints that would let experts reconstruct it. He calls it Kolmogorov complexity2 modulo experts. For the unit-distance problem, his hint sequence had three parts: Look for a counterexample. Take the best known construction and generalize it. Try a sequence of number fields of increasing degree, but work with prime ideals of bounded norm. items.why_it_matters: An essay on frontier models solving hard math problems. It is interesting for capability trends but has little near-term engineering impact.

items.title: [AINews] Black October
items.author: swyx .ai
items.excerpt: If you are reading this, you’re receiving this from our new provider, Beehiiv! We are making progress on our redesign — if you have a friend that didn’t receive AINews, please find us in Spam filter and move us out to your Inbox… thank you! AINews is now free… we are building new subscriber benefits soon. We ordinarily try not to repeat title stories if we already covered it, as we did Patch the Planet yesterday and our Cyber trend call in July. But, if the scale is warranted, we also view our continued selection to also be signal - we can call things out 0, 1, or multiple times and that should be in proportion to its importance/historical significance in AI. We last did this with OpenClaw. “Black October” counts as such. Here’s a list:View post on X ↗AI News for 10/21/2026-10/22/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapBlack October: AI-Accelerated Vulnerability Disclosures Overwhelm DefendersScale of the incident wave: Over roughly 48 hours, a cluster of critical disclosures and breaches landed together (summary, roundup, patch list). Core software: PHP2Shell is an unauthenticated RCE in PHP. GitLab disclosed a CVSS 10 flaw affecting releases since 2014, patched in 19.5.1. Node.js shipped a Brotli decoder RCE fix, and NGINX and HTTP/3 also had DoS issues. Supply chain: LiteLLM 1.107.0 shipped with a password stealer. Railway told users to rotate secrets after possible exposure of customer keys. Zeabur is shutting down after 321,810 accounts were breached. Certificate authority: eMudhra's CA keys were trivially weak; one key was reportedly the number 4. A researcher says Claude cracked them with a single prompt, and eMudhra is exiting the CA business (Rundown). Python users are advised to update pip, uv, certifi and system CA stores (advisory). Healthcare data: Quest Diagnostics
items.why_it_matters: Appears to cover a large wave of security incidents and patching this month. Worth checking for exposure in our stack and supply chain, though the excerpt gives few details.

items.title: [AINews] Kimi 3.1 Pro 104BA-2.8T: Fable-5.1-Class Open Weights narrows Closed-AI lead to 1 month... and Pro Highspeed API with 2-3× speed
items.author: swyx .ai
items.excerpt: 2 months ago we covered Z.ai CEO Prof Jie Tang’s prediction that we’d get a Fable-class open weights model by year end. 2 weeks ago Meta achieved a Fable-class model in closed source, but, with 2.5 months left to go, we finally got it - a 2.8T open weights model beating Fable 5.1, not just Fable 5, at that: View post on X ↗ with even better efficiency: View post on X ↗ You can tell Kimi is proud of their latest model by how fancy their landing page is: As usual we don’t get much research detail - the update is somewhat similar to Z.ai’s 5.2-5.3 bump - a minor version bump for a lot more post-training: Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains, we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain.AI News for 10/22/2026-10/23/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords.
